samples.text:
The diagram shows how the raw wool from sheep is processed into yarn. There are eight stages in the process.

Firstly, the fleece is removed from the sheep in spring, this is called shearing. Then the dirty edges of the wool are removed and the wool is graded by its quality. After that, the wool is washed in warm soapy water for removing the grease. This stage is called scouring.

Next, the wool is dried by warm air. Then the fibres are combed so they are straight, and they make a soft web. This is carding. After that, the fibres are twisted and they become yarn, which is called spinning.

In the seventh stage, the yarn is dyed in large vats, so it have colour. Finally, the yarn is wound into balls or into cones.

Overall, the process start with the sheep and it ends with yarn which is ready to use. Most of stages are about cleaning the wool and making it into yarn, and the colour is added near the end of the process.
samples.why: Basic overview placed at the end · all eight stages covered in order · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · agreement and article errors plus a comma splice, meaning always clear.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates the stages through which raw sheep's wool passes before it becomes yarn.

Overall, the process is linear and consists of eight stages. The first half involves removing the wool from the sheep and cleaning it, while the second half focuses on turning the fibres into yarn, colouring it and winding it.

The process begins in spring, when the fleece is sheared from the sheep. During skirting and grading, the dirty edges are cut away and the wool is graded according to the quality. It is then scoured, meaning that it is washed in warm soapy water to remove grease, and afterwards it is dried using warm air.

In the carding stage, the fibres are combed straight to create a soft web, and these fibres are then twisted into yarn during spinning. Following this, the yarn is coloured in large vats in the dyeing stage, before finally being wound into balls or cones. This means that the colour is added only after the yarn has been made. At this point, the yarn is ready to be used, for example for knitting or weaving.
samples.why: Clear overview dividing the process into two halves · logical sequencing with passive forms · appropriate vocabulary (sheared, scoured, vats) · mostly error-free with one article slip.

samples.text:
The diagram depicts the process by which fleece shorn from sheep is transformed into finished yarn.

In total, there are eight stages, which can be broadly divided into two phases: the first four prepare and clean the raw wool, whereas the final four convert the clean fibres into yarn that is coloured and wound for use.

The process starts in spring, when sheep are sheared and their fleece is removed. This is followed by skirting and grading, in which the soiled edges are trimmed off and the wool is sorted according to its quality. The wool is then scoured in warm, soapy water to strip away grease, and subsequently dried with warm air. These preparatory steps ensure that the wool is clean before any processing of the fibres begins.

Once dry, the wool is carded, a step in which the fibres are combed straight into a soft web. These fibres are then spun, meaning they are twisted together to form yarn. The yarn is dyed in large vats and, in the final stage, wound into balls or cones, at which point it is ready for use.
samples.why: Insightful overview splitting the process into two phases · every stage covered with precise terminology (skirting, scoured, carded) · cohesion managed smoothly · wide range of structures · error-free.
